name: Hair dye / bleaching

lead: Hair dye and bleach change hair color on the spot: lighter, darker, or gray covered. In style circles they are used to change contrast with the skin and eyes and give a visibly new look. Reports say 50 to 80 percent of women in the US, Europe and Japan have used hair dye.

Permanent dye and bleach use an oxidizer and an alkaline agent such as ammonia to open the hair cuticle; bleach oxidizes melanin to lighten, while dye deposits color. Lower-strength dyes coat or lightly penetrate the hair without lightening. The techniques are well established, though no studies test whether coloring improves attractiveness.

paras: People color at a salon or at home, with bleach followed by toner for lighter shades and a permanent or semi-permanent dye for darker or natural-looking color. Roots need touching up as hair grows, and bleached hair is usually given extra conditioning.

Reported risks are skin irritation, PPD allergy, hair breakage, skin staining and unexpected color. Studies linking dye to cancer are limited and inconsistent, and the EU restricts about 45 hair dye chemicals.

chain: Different contrast with skin and eyes
angle.text: Bleaching hair lighter or dyeing it darker changes your contrast with your skin and eyes and covers gray, and the new color is visible immediately. Hair coloring is a well-established cosmetic method used by a large share of adults.

lead: Hair dye and bleaching change the color of head hair. People use them to cover gray, to match hair to a skin tone or style, or to shift contrast, for example dyeing hair a darker shade or bleaching it lighter. Looksmaxxing forum members discuss both as a way to change how the hair frames the face, and also use dye on brows, lashes and facial hair.[1][2][3]

Bleaching lightens hair by oxidizing melanin, typically with hydrogen peroxide and an alkaline agent such as ammonia.[1] Dyes deposit color in or on the hair shaft. Permanent dyes use an oxidizing developer, while semi-permanent and temporary dyes stain the hair without lightening it.[1][4] Dye use is widespread: reports cited by Wikipedia say 50 to 80 percent of women in the US, Europe and Japan have used it.[1]

Documented downsides include scalp irritation, allergy to p-phenylenediamine (PPD), breakage and unexpected tones. The US National Cancer Institute describes research on personal hair dye use and cancer as mixed.[1][4]

paras: Permanent dye uses ammonia and an oxidizing developer to open the hair cuticle and form pigment in the cortex. The National Cancer Institute notes that permanent products make up about 80 percent of those marketed and work by reacting colorless intermediates with hydrogen peroxide.[4] Demi-permanent dye uses a lower peroxide level and cannot lighten hair, and semi-permanent dye lasts roughly 4 to 8 shampoos. Temporary products wash out in one shampoo.[1]
Vivid or fashion colors contain tint but no developer, so on dark hair they usually require bleaching first.[1]
Bleaching breaks down melanin by oxidation, releasing oxygen gas. Bleached hair can turn brassy or yellow, and toners and purple shampoos are used to correct undertones.[1]

A looksmax.org poster who bleached already light-blond hair reported that it reached near-white after toning and showed little visible regrowth, while another member in the same thread said bleach is permanent but can leave hair in poor texture for people who start dark and need long processing.[5]

Threads on looksmax.org include members asking how to dye hair while limiting damage, how to go from ginger to black, and which dark shade matches the look of their hair when wet.[2][3][6] Other threads discuss dyeing brows, lashes and facial hair, and how to judge whether black or dark brown will suit a complexion.[7][8]
Skin bleaching and tooth bleaching are separate practices that share the word and are discussed in their own entries.

Hair dye recipes appear in Assyrian herbals from about 2177 BCE, and the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describes dyeing gray hair. Diodorus Siculus described Celtic peoples bleaching hair with lime.[1] Perkin's discovery of mauveine in 1856 launched synthetic dyes, Eugene Schueller is credited with the first synthetic hair dye in 1907, and Schwarzkopf launched a home color product in 1947.[1] The NCI reports that manufacturers changed permanent dye formulas in the mid to late 1970s to remove some intermediates found to be carcinogenic in animals.[4]

Dye can cause skin irritation, allergic reactions, hair breakage and skin staining. PPD-based dyes have been controversial, symptoms can appear hours to a day later, and manufacturers recommend patch testing, which some European dermatologists advise against for self-testing.[1]

In 2010 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classed some chemicals encountered by hairdressers as probably carcinogenic, while personal hair dye use was judged not classifiable. The NCI describes results for bladder cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and breast cancer as mixed or inconsistent.[4] The EU restricts about 45 chemicals in hair dyes.[1] A 2024 case report in JAMA Ophthalmology described retinopathy associated with hair dye.[9]

No studies found testing hair color change as a means of improving attractiveness. Epidemiological studies on hair dye use and health include the Copenhagen City Heart Study (2016, 7,684 women followed for 37 years) and a 2018 meta-analysis on breast cancer risk.[1] The NCI summarizes a 2014 pooled analysis of 17 studies that found no increased bladder cancer risk with personal use, and a 2020 cohort that found no association with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.[4] Studies of dental bleaching, found in the same literature, concern teeth rather than hair.
